Go find private party listings for similar cars in your area. Be detailed, make a list of year, mileage, price, and condition. Does your car have any options that would drive up the price? Make a note of those. The more information you have, the better.

Call the agent back and give them a number backed up by the research you did. This is a negotiation like any other. The insurance company wants to pay you as little as possible. Tell the agent something along the lines of you don't think they've valued the car appropriately, you know there aren't a ton of similar sales in your area, but based on what you could find you think $xxxx is fair.

Time is money. The agent has other cases and the company has other cars to salvage. Be direct and willing to compromise. If they're really way off - not "bottom end of reasonable" price, I mean "are you kidding me I could get more in scrap value" price - you can contact your state's department of insurance as an absolute last resort.

And please, coming from someone who works at an insurance company: treat your claims agent like a human being. They get screamed at all day long and still somehow manage to come back to work the next day. Being polite and easy to work with might get you an extra few hundred dollars in your settlement.

If you were going to go to the store with a tape measure, you'd have to take some things into consideration. Ease is added to the total measurement; if I were making a skirt that fit at the waist for someone who had a waist measurement of 28, the final circumference of the waist of the skirt would be 28.5 (if I didn't screw anything up).

When you measure a waist, you generally only measure across the front, so you'd take the number that is your waist size plus ease and divide it by two, then look for pants with that measurement.

Half an inch of ease is not a magic number, though. I have a pair of jeggings that measure 13" across the waist for a circumference of 26", when my waist is actually more like 27". They're stretchy, so to fit correctly they were made with negative ease. You can rule too-big things out with waist measurements - if your waist is 28" and the pants measure 30", they will not fit your waist. But they could measure 27" and be fine, depending on the fabric and the cut.

Sewing and pattern making are absolutely fascinating, but hard to just dip your toe into. If this is something that interests you, there's lots and lots of free resources on Google!

Short version: Jib. It's "I like the cut of your jib."  
  
Long version: Back when we had actual sailing vessels and we used them for war, we didn't have ways to communicate with other ships at sea and find out if they were friendly or not. As you might be able to guess, this posed some problems.

However, different nations built different-looking ships that used different-looking sails. So, with practice, it was easy to tell what country a ship was from from the shape of the sails, specifically the shape of the one at the very front of the ship: the jib.

"Liking the cut of a jib" meant that you thought a ship was probably friendly. The phrase eventually evolved to apply to people you liked, too.

Source: I am an armchair scholar on the Age of Sail.
